text: Later, she completed her Ph.D. and started teaching. Why do you think she chose to teach as a career? In what way would her experiences in these jobs be different from each other? question 28 Kimmerer is active in conservation and ecology projects. She has been involved with the Strategies for Ecology Education, Development and Sustainability project, Ecological Society of America Traditional Ecological Knowledge Section, and has even participated in a discussion at a United Nations meeting on ecology. What are the advantages of these programs? Why were these programs implemented? Why did the author choose to be a part of these programs? question 29 Kimmerer is the director of the Center for Native Peoples and the Environment , an initiative geared towards sharing of modern environmental science and traditional environmental knowledge. How does this help people in general? Can Native American traditional environmental knowledge help people in China, Nigeria, or India, or do these countries require different environmental perspectives? Why, or why not? question 30 Kimmerer’s first book, Gathering Moss: A Natural and Cultural History of Mosses, received the John Burroughs Medal Award. Her second book, Braiding Sweetgrass: Indigenous Wisdom, Scientific Knowledge and the Teachings of Plants , is the recipient of the 2014 Sigurd F. Olson Nature Writing Award. What is the value of such awards for books? What other awards would you nominate Kimmerer for? question 31 A special hardcover edition of Braiding Sweetgrass was published with a new introduction from Robin Wall Kimmerer in honor of the fortieth anniversary of Milkweed Editions. The book was reissued as an object of meaning that will last for a long time. Why do you think the publishing company chose this book for its anniversary reissue? question 32 Despite its success, Braiding Sweetgrass did not have a large-scale marketing campaign. Instead, it became popular through “word of mouth” and recommendations from one reader to the other. Why do you think some books do not require a large marketing campaign and still become a huge hit? What is it about Braiding Sweetgrass that it became a success? question 33 The few criticisms of the book state that the stories run together and are often repetitive, and the author’s presentation of the subject is completely one-sided, not taking into account the social problems of indigenous or traditional societies. What is your major criticism of Braiding Sweetgrass ? How could the book have been improved? Explain and discuss. question 34 The cover is designed by Tony Drehfal and contains an engraving as well as a deckled edge and a bookmark ribbon. The new edition also contains five colorful illustrations by artist Nate Christopherson. In what way does the cover complement the subject matter of Braiding Sweetgrass ? Is it important to have a cover that represents the content of the book? Discuss. question 35 Braiding Sweetgrass won the 2014 Sigurd F. Olson Nature Writing Award, given in honor of the literary legacy of Sigurd F. Olson to the best environmental writings in adult nonfiction and children’s literature. Why do you think it merited this award? question 36 The name, Braiding Sweetgrass , is a metaphor referring to the fact that the stories told in the book are made up of three strands: the traditional indigenous perspective about the environment, scientific knowledge about plants, and the beauty of the knowledge that plants themselves hold and can teach those who want to learn. If you were to suggest an alternative name for this book, what would it be and why do you think it would be suitable? question 37 Kimmerer has written two books so far: Gathering Moss: A Natural and Cultural History of Mosses and Braiding Sweetgrass: Indigenous Wisdom, Scientific Knowledge and the Teachings of Plants . What should be the topic of her next book, if you were to choose for her, and why? question 38 Kimmerer talks about the bounty of strawberries and how she could call herself “raised by strawberries.” If you were to have a plant that could have raised you, which one would it be? Why do you think so? question 39 Kimmerer desires to connect back to her roots. A trained botanist, she desires to combine her scientific knowledge with traditional knowledge. She had also begun to take Potawatomi classes, of which there were only nine fluent speakers left at the time, and became a member of the Potawatomi Nation. If you were in her place, what measures would you take to reconnect with your lost heritage? Why do you think these steps would help you? question 40 A member of the Potawatomi Nation, Kimmerer is a botany professor and tries to mingle the two worldviews, scientific and traditional ecological knowledge, for a better understanding of plants. If Kimmerer were not a Native American, how do you think her relationship with plants would be, and why? Would it be similar or different? Why? question 41 Kimmerer grew up in a rural area where she interacted every day with plants in the garden, woods, or even the wetlands. This led to a deep and sustained interest in the diverse biological world around her. She thought of plants as companions and assigned them real-life roles that help people along. How do you think this book would have been different if she had been brought up in a city? question 42 Kimmerer’s family was a part of the exodus of Native Americans from their homelands to less fertile lands. Her grandfather, Asa Wall, was forcibly sent to the Carlisle Indian Industrial School and deliberately and systematically uprooted from his people and traditional way of life. In what way would the world be different if colonization had not happened? How would native Europeans relate to other cultures in this context? question 43 The cover for Braiding Sweetgrass is designed by Tony Drehfal and contains an engraving as well as a deckled edge and a bookmark ribbon.
